name: Naki
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

earlier_scan.source_named: Kum Nang, Julius. 2002. A sketch-phonology and a step towards the standardization of Naki. (Yaounde ms.)
earlier_scan.note: Kum 2002 sketch-phonology not online; Good's online Naki Grammar Sketch (read, 6pp) covers tone only, no stress statement

sources.citation: Good, Jeff, Jesse Lovegren, Jean Patrick Mve, Carine Nganguep Tchiemouo, Rebecca Voll & Pierpaolo Di Carlo. 2011. The languages of the Lower Fungom region of Cameroon: Grammatical overview. Africana Linguistica 17: 101-164. DOI 10.2143/AL.17.0.2146552 (text read from Persee per-page fragments; PDF endpoint captcha-blocked; page images of pp.151-154 saved)
sources.note: Nothing. Sec. 3.7.2 Naki phonology (pp.152-154): consonants, vowels, 3.7.2.3 Tones p.154 'There is clear evidence for the presence of four tone levels in Naki... Contour tones are also frequently encountered'. No mention of stress or accent anywhere in the Naki section (only 'stress' hit in the article is rhetorical 'It should be stressed that...').

sources.citation: Kum, Julius Nang. 2002. A sketch phonology and a step towards the standardization of Naki. Maitrise dissertation, Department of African Languages and Linguistics, FALSH, University of Yaounde I. ix+124 pp. (MPG PuRe item_403539, hdl:11858/00-001M-0000-0012-7FF2-5; PDF public via PuRe REST API)
sources.access_detail: copy on file; access check: not located online or at Harvard
sources.note: Nothing. Whole thesis is phonology (ch.1 Tones, ch.2 Vowels, ch.3 Consonants, ch.4 Syllables, ch.5 Tone distribution/function, ch.6-7 standardization and orthography); no stress/accent section or remark found (TOC read from page images; scanned layer grepped; ch.1, ch.4, ch.5, ch.7 read). p.21: 'Naki is a tone language. This implies the language uses tones to distinguish the meaning of words.' Two level tones H, L plus contour LH, HL; tone marks singular/plural and tense.

sources.citation: Good, Jeff & Jesse Lovegren. 2017. Remarks on the nasal classes in Mungbam and Naki. In R. Kramer & R. Kiessling (eds.), Mechthildian approaches to Afrikanistik. Koln: Koppe (preprint, 8 pp.).

Good, Jeff. 2013. A (micro-)accretion zone in a remnant zone? Lower Fungom in areal-historical perspective. In Bickel et al. (eds.), Language Typology and Historical Contingency, 265-282. Amsterdam: Benjamins (preprint).

Good, Jeff. 2010. Topic and focus fields in Naki. In Ines Fiedler & Anne Schwarz (eds.), The Expression of Information Structure: A documentation of its diversity across Africa, 35-68. Amsterdam: Benjamins (author preprint).
sources.note: Nothing on Naki word stress; the one 'accent placement' mention refers to English (Lambrecht 1994). Notes an emphatic 3sg pronoun with 'a much more articulated tone contour' post-verbally (intonation/focus, not word stress).

sources.note: Nothing. Sec. 2 Phonology: segment inventory; 2.2 Tone system 'essentially unanalyzed', three tone levels (H, M, L), some monosyllabic contours, nasals not tone-bearing. No stress/accent statement.

sources.note: Good is the only linguist with sustained fieldwork on Naki; an unpublished tonal/prosodic analysis, if it exists, would be the place a stress or accent observation appears. KPAAM-CAM output list (checked) shows no Naki phonology thesis to date.
